aenon.text: The springs of the upper Jordan Valley near Salim, east of Nablus, still feed small streams and farm plots. A Byzantine pilgrim map, the Madaba mosaic, marks "Aenon near Salim" here; no church stands at the spot today.

cana.text: Kafr Kanna, a town of about 25,000 near Nazareth, is the traditional Cana. Its Franciscan Wedding Church, built in 1881, keeps old stone jars, and couples come to renew their vows. Many scholars prefer Khirbet Qana, an unbuilt ruin 5 miles north.
cana.credit: The Franciscan Wedding Church at Kafr Kanna. Photo: Chris06, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

capernaum.text: Capernaum is an excavated village on the north shore of the lake. A white limestone synagogue of the 4th or 5th century stands over the black basalt footings of an older one, and a modern church on stilts, built in 1990, hovers over the house honored as Peter's.
capernaum.credit: The white synagogue at Capernaum. Photo: Berthold Werner, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

galilee.text: Lower Galilee is now a region of Arab and Jewish towns, olive groves and wheat fields between Nazareth and the lake. The Jesus Trail, opened in 2008, links Nazareth, Cana and Capernaum on foot over about 40 miles.
galilee.credit: A lookout tower on Mount Turan, Lower Galilee. Photo: שלמה רודד, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

jacobswell.text: Jacob's Well lies in Bir Ya'qub, on the east edge of Nablus in the West Bank. A Greek Orthodox church, finished in 2007 over Crusader and Byzantine foundations, shelters the well, which still gives water from about 130 feet down.
jacobswell.credit: Christ Pantocrator in the dome of the church at Jacob's Well. Photo: Victorgrigas, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

judeacountry.text: The Judean hills north and west of Jerusalem are terraced with olives and vines around Palestinian villages and Israeli settlements. The old paths between the villages still follow the ridges.
judeacountry.credit: An old stone terrace in the Judean hills. Photo: ekeidar, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

judeanwild.text: The Greek Orthodox Monastery of the Temptation clings to the cliff of Mount Quarantania above Jericho, built in 1895 over caves used by hermits since the 4th century. A cable car from Jericho runs up near it.
judeanwild.credit: The Monastery of the Temptation above Jericho. Photo: Daniel Case, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

machaerus.text: Machaerus is a hilltop ruin in Jordan, above the Dead Sea near the village of Mukawir. Excavations since 1968 have uncovered Herod's palace, a courtyard and baths; a single re-erected column marks the site.
machaerus.credit: The hill of Machaerus above the Dead Sea. Photo: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

beatitudes.text: The Church of the Beatitudes, an octagonal domed church by Antonio Barluzzi finished in 1938, stands on the hill above Tabgha. Its eight sides recall the eight Beatitudes, and its gardens look down over the lake.
beatitudes.credit: The Church of the Beatitudes. Photo: Fallaner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

bethesda.text: The excavated Pool of Bethesda lies in the grounds of the Crusader Church of St Anne, near the Lions' Gate of the Old City. Deep basins, Roman and Byzantine arches and the ruins of a 5th-century church can be seen together.
bethesda.credit: Ruins at the Pool of Bethesda. Photo: James Emery from Douglasville, United States, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

kursi.text: Kursi National Park, on the east shore of the lake, holds the ruins of a large 5th-century monastery with mosaic floors, found during road building in 1970. A small chapel up the hillside marks the traditional place of the swine.
kursi.credit: The monastery ruins at Kursi. Photo: זאב שטיין, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

nain.text: Nein is a small Arab village on the north slope of the Hill of Moreh. A small Franciscan church, built in 1880 on older ruins, recalls the raising of the widow's son.

seagalilee.text: The lake, also called Kinneret or Tiberias, is about 13 miles long and 700 feet below sea level. Fishing still goes on, and wooden tourist boats cross between Tiberias and Ginosar, near where a 1st-century fishing boat was found in 1986.
seagalilee.credit: A wooden tour boat on the Sea of Galilee. Photo: Lux Moundi, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

tabgha.text: Tabgha on the north-west shore has two churches: the Church of the Multiplication, rebuilt in 1982 around the 5th-century mosaic of loaves and fishes, and the small black basalt Church of the Primacy of Peter, built in 1933.
tabgha.credit: The Church of the Multiplication at Tabgha. Photo: David Shankbone, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

bethany.text: Bethany is the West Bank town of al-Eizariya, whose Arabic name keeps Lazarus's. Steps lead down into the tomb honored as his, and a Franciscan church by Antonio Barluzzi, finished in 1954, stands beside it. The separation barrier now cuts the old road to Jerusalem.
bethany.credit: The entrance to the Tomb of Lazarus, al-Eizariya. Photo: Abraham, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

bethsaida.text: Two sites compete for Bethsaida: et-Tell, a mound north of the lake excavated since 1987, and el-Araj, nearer the shore, where a Byzantine church was found in 2019. Both lie in the Bethsaida Valley nature reserve.

burqin.text: Burqin is a Palestinian village west of Jenin. Its Church of St George, among the oldest in the land, is built around a cave where tradition says Jesus healed the ten lepers.
burqin.credit: The Church of St George at Burqin. Photo: محمد عليان جميل, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

caesareaphil.text: Banias, at the foot of Mount Hermon, is a nature reserve. A spring flows from below a great cave and niches cut for Pan, and the ruins of Herod Philip's city and a later palace lie along the stream.
caesareaphil.credit: Ruins at Banias, ancient Caesarea Philippi. Photo: Fallaner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

decapolis.text: The Decapolis cities now lie mostly in northern Jordan. Jerash (Gerasa) is one of the best-preserved Roman cities anywhere, with colonnaded streets and theatres; Umm Qais (Gadara) looks down on the Sea of Galilee.
decapolis.credit: Ruins of Gadara at Umm Qais, Jordan. Photo: Samir I. Sharbaty, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

ephraim.text: Taybeh, a Christian village north-east of Jerusalem, is often identified with Ephraim. It is known for its churches, the ruins of the Byzantine Church of St George, and a brewery.

gennesaret.text: The Plain of Gennesaret, between Magdala and Tabgha, is still farmed, with banana groves and orchards. Kibbutz Ginosar keeps the Galilee Boat, a 1st-century fishing boat found in the mud in 1986.

hermon.text: Mount Hermon, 9,232 feet high, is shared by Syria, Lebanon and the Israeli-held Golan Heights. Its upper slopes carry snow much of the year, and Israel's only ski area operates there.
hermon.credit: Snow on the slopes of Mount Hermon. Photo: Nunusandio, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

magdala.text: Magdala's 1st-century town was excavated from 2009, when a synagogue with a carved stone table, the Magdala Stone, was found. The Duc in Altum center beside it, opened in 2014, has a boat-shaped altar looking over the lake.
magdala.credit: The excavated 1st-century synagogue at Magdala. Photo: Bahnfrend, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

olives.text: The Mount of Olives is covered by the great Jewish cemetery, with churches on its slopes: the Dominus Flevit chapel, shaped like a teardrop, and the Church of All Nations at its foot. Its top gives the classic view across the Kidron to the Old City.
olives.credit: The Mount of Olives from the air. Photo: Godot13, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

perea.text: Perea is now the Jordan Valley and hill country of western Jordan. The Baptism Site, Bethany beyond the Jordan, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015.

samariavillage.text: The hills of Samaria are now the northern West Bank, around Nablus and Jenin. A few hundred Samaritans still live on Mount Gerizim and in Holon, keeping their Passover sacrifice on the mountain.
samariavillage.credit: The hills of Samaria. Photo: Orrling, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

siloam.text: The Pool of Siloam of Jesus' day was uncovered by chance in 2004, when a pipe was repaired in the City of David. Its broad steps are being excavated, and the ancient Pilgrim Road from the pool up to the Temple has been opened beside it.
siloam.credit: The excavated steps of the Pool of Siloam. Photo: Ian Scott, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

tyre.text: Tyre (Sour) and Sidon (Saida) are coastal cities of southern Lebanon. Tyre's Roman ruins, with a great hippodrome and colonnaded street, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
tyre.credit: Roman ruins at Tyre. Photo: Oussama Tahmaz, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

akeldama.text: Akeldama lies on the south slope of the Hinnom Valley, below the Old City. The Greek Orthodox Monastery of St Onuphrius is built among old rock-cut tombs there.

bethphage.text: Bethphage, on the east slope of the Mount of Olives, has a Franciscan church of 1883 with a stone painted with the scene of the colt. The Palm Sunday procession to Jerusalem begins from here each year.
bethphage.credit: The apse painting of the entry into Jerusalem at the church of Bethphage. Photo: Kenad, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

caiaphas.text: On Mount Zion, the Church of St Peter in Gallicantu, finished in 1931, stands over caves and a pit honored as the place of Jesus' night in custody. Ancient stone steps, perhaps of the 1st century, lead down the hill beside it.
caiaphas.credit: St Peter in Gallicantu, Mount Zion. Photo: Zairon, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

gethsemane.text: Gethsemane is a small garden of ancient olive trees at the foot of the Mount of Olives. Beside it the Church of All Nations, finished in 1924 with gifts from many countries, keeps the Rock of the Agony before its altar.
gethsemane.credit: Old olive trees in the Garden of Gethsemane. Photo: Beko, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

golgotha.text: Golgotha is inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, in the Christian Quarter. Steep steps lead up to the Rock of Calvary, now in a chapel shared by Catholics and Greek Orthodox; the rock can be touched through a hole under the altar.
golgotha.credit: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre. Photo: Mohammad Shad Siddiqui, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

herodpalace.text: The site of Herod's palace is on the west side of the Old City, by the Jaffa Gate. The Citadel, the Tower of David, stands on its northern towers and holds the Tower of David Museum.
herodpalace.credit: The Citadel (Tower of David) by the Jaffa Gate. Photo: Bukvoed, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

praetorium.text: Pilate's Praetorium was probably Herod's palace by the Jaffa Gate, where excavations under the Kishle building have shown its foundations. The Via Dolorosa, though, begins at the Antonia, by the Lions' Gate, following a medieval tradition.
praetorium.credit: The Via Dolorosa in the Old City. Photo: Fallaner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

tomb.text: The tomb is enclosed in the Edicule, a small shrine in the rotunda of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. Its restoration in 2016–2017 opened the burial bench for the first time in centuries and found the rock beneath.

upperroom.text: The Cenacle on Mount Zion is a Gothic hall of the 14th century, built by the Franciscans in the Crusader style. Beneath it is the place honored as the Tomb of David, and a minaret recalls its time as a mosque.
upperroom.credit: The Gothic hall of the Cenacle on Mount Zion. Photo: Chris06, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

emmaus.text: Several places claim Emmaus. Emmaus Nicopolis, in Canada Park west of Jerusalem, has Byzantine and Crusader church ruins; Abu Ghosh and El Qubeibeh, closer to Luke's distance, also keep churches of Emmaus.
emmaus.credit: Church ruins at Emmaus Nicopolis. Photo: Bukvoed, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

galileemount.text: Tradition has placed the mountain of the Great Commission on Mount Tabor or above Tabgha by the lake. Neither is certain; Matthew gives only "the mountain to which Jesus had directed them."

jerusalem.text: Jerusalem today is a city of nearly a million people. The walled Old City, rebuilt by Suleiman the Magnificent in the 1530s, holds the Jewish, Christian, Muslim and Armenian quarters.
jerusalem.credit: The Old City from the Mount of Olives. Photo: brionv from San Francisco, United States, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

jerusalemchurch.text: Jerusalem today is a city of nearly a million people. The walled Old City, rebuilt by Suleiman the Magnificent in the 1530s, keeps more than forty churches of a dozen Christian communities.
jerusalemchurch.credit: The Old City walls and the Tower of David. Photo: Pudelek, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stephensite.text: Two places honor Stephen: the Lions' Gate, also called St Stephen's Gate, and the Dominican École Biblique north of Damascus Gate, whose church stands on the 5th-century basilica built by the Empress Eudocia.
stephensite.credit: The Lions' Gate, also called St Stephen's Gate. Photo: Djampa, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

antioch.text: Antioch is Antakya in southern Turkey. Its Cave Church of St Peter on Mount Staurin is one of the oldest church sites anywhere. Much of the city was destroyed in the earthquake of February 2023 and is being rebuilt.
antioch.credit: The Cave Church of St Peter, Antakya. Photo: Dosseman, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

arabia.text: Paul's Arabia was the Nabataean kingdom, now southern Jordan and the Negev. Its capital Petra, carved in red sandstone, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and Jordan's most visited place.
arabia.credit: The desert of Wadi Rum, in the Nabataean south. Photo: Peter Chisholm, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

damascus.text: Damascus is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. Straight Street (Via Recta) still crosses the Old City, and the Chapel of Ananias lies underground near its eastern end, the Bab Sharqi.
damascus.credit: A street near Straight Street in the Old City of Damascus. Photo: Fede Renghino, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

gazaroad.text: The old road from Jerusalem down to Gaza ran through the Shephelah, the low hills between the mountains and the coastal plain. Beit Guvrin, with its caves and ruins, is one of the places along it.

joppa.text: Old Jaffa is now part of Tel Aviv. St Peter's Church, built in 1654 and rebuilt in 1894, rises over the harbor, and a house in the old lanes is shown as Simon the Tanner's.
joppa.credit: The old port of Jaffa. Photo: Noam.armonn, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

kawkab.text: Kawkab, south-west of Damascus, has a Greek Orthodox monastery commemorating Paul's conversion. The Syrian war has kept most visitors away since 2011.

lydda.text: Lydda is Lod, a city near Ben Gurion Airport. The Church of St George, rebuilt in 1870 over the saint's traditional tomb, stands beside the al-Khidr mosque.
lydda.credit: The Church of St George, Lod. Photo: תומר א., free use with attribution, via Wikimedia Commons

sebaste.text: Sebastia is a Palestinian village north-west of Nablus. Herod's temple to Augustus, a colonnaded street and a theatre lie in ruins, and a Crusader cathedral, later a mosque, honors the tomb of John the Baptist.
sebaste.credit: The Roman theatre at Sebastia. Photo: Daniel Ventura, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

tarsus.text: Tarsus is a city of some 350,000 in southern Turkey. St Paul's Well and a stretch of Roman road are shown to visitors, and the Church of St Paul, now a museum, is open for pilgrim services.
tarsus.credit: The Roman gate called Cleopatra's Gate, Tarsus. Photo: Dosseman, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

attalia.text: Attalia is Antalya, one of Turkey's busiest resort cities. Its walled old town, Kaleiçi, keeps Hadrian's Gate, built in AD 130, and the old Roman harbor.
attalia.credit: Hadrian's Gate, Antalya. Photo: Bernard Gagnon, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

derbe.text: Derbe's mound, Kerti Hüyük, lies near Karaman in central Turkey. It is unexcavated farmland; inscriptions found nearby in 1956 and 1962 named the city.

iconium.text: Iconium is Konya, a large Turkish city best known for the tomb of the poet Rumi. The small Church of St Paul in the city center, built in 1910, still serves a Catholic community.

lystra.text: Lystra is a low mound near the village of Hatunsaray, south-west of Konya. It is almost unexcavated; a Latin inscription found in 1885 identified the site.

paphos.text: Paphos, on the south-west coast of Cyprus, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its Roman villas and floor mosaics. St Paul's Pillar, by the church of Agia Kyriaki Chrysopolitissa, is shown as the place he was scourged.
paphos.credit: A Roman floor mosaic at Paphos. Photo: Friedhelm Dröge, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

perga.text: Perga is an extensive ruin near Antalya, with a stadium, theatre, colonnaded streets and Hellenistic gate towers. It is one of the best-preserved ancient cities in Turkey.
perga.credit: The ruins of Perga through a Roman arch. Photo: Alexey Komarov, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

pisidianantioch.text: Pisidian Antioch is a ruin just outside Yalvaç in central Turkey. Its excavated remains include a temple of Augustus, an aqueduct and the foundations of a large 4th-century church.

salamis.text: Salamis, north of Famagusta in northern Cyprus, is a large ruined city with a gymnasium, baths and theatre. The Monastery of St Barnabas, nearby, keeps the tomb honored as his.
salamis.credit: Columns of the Roman gymnasium at Salamis. Photo: Michal Klajban, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

athens.text: The Areopagus is a bare marble outcrop below the Acropolis, worn smooth by visitors. A bronze plaque at the foot of its steps carries Paul's speech from Acts 17 in Greek.
athens.credit: The Areopagus seen from the Acropolis. Photo: Jakub Hałun, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

beroea.text: Beroea is Veria in northern Greece. A modern shrine with mosaics, the Bema of St Paul, marks the steps where tradition says he preached.
beroea.credit: Veria, ancient Beroea. Photo: Zisis Tsampalis, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

cenchreae.text: Cenchreae, Corinth's eastern port, is now Kechries, a small bay. Remains of the ancient harbor, including a Christian church, can be seen in the shallow water.
cenchreae.credit: The ancient harbor at Kechries. Photo: George E. Koronaios, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

corinth.text: Ancient Corinth is an excavated city below the great rock of Acrocorinth. Its forum keeps the Bema, the speaker's platform where Paul is believed to have stood before Gallio.
corinth.credit: The Temple of Apollo at Ancient Corinth, below Acrocorinth. Photo: George E. Koronaios, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

ephesus.text: Ephesus is one of the largest Roman ruins in the Mediterranean, near Selçuk. The great theatre of Acts 19 seats about 24,000, and the restored Library of Celsus faces the marble street.
ephesus.credit: The Library of Celsus, Ephesus. Photo: Herbert Weber, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

philippi.text: Philippi is a ruin and UNESCO World Heritage Site in eastern Macedonia. A baptistery by the Zygaktis stream marks where Lydia is said to have been baptized.
philippi.credit: Ruins of a Byzantine basilica at Philippi. Photo: Berthold Werner, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

phrygia.text: Phrygia and Galatia are now the central Anatolian plateau, a land of wheat fields, steppe and small towns. Ankara, ancient Ancyra and capital of Galatia, is now the capital of Turkey.
phrygia.credit: Fields on the Anatolian plateau. Photo: Alen Ištoković, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

thessalonica.text: Thessalonica is Thessaloniki, Greece's second city. Its Roman and Byzantine monuments, including the Rotunda and the Church of St Demetrius, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
thessalonica.credit: The Arch of Galerius and the Rotunda, Thessaloniki. Photo: Falk2, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

troas.text: Alexandria Troas is a ruin among oak woods on the Aegean coast of Turkey. Parts of its baths, walls and silted harbor remain.
troas.credit: The Roman baths at Alexandria Troas. Photo: Elelicht, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

assos.text: Assos is the village of Behramkale, on the Gulf of Edremit. A Doric temple of Athena crowns the hill, and the old harbor below is now a small fishing port.

macedonia.text: Macedonia is the northern region of modern Greece. The Egnatian Way, the Roman road Paul walked, can still be traced near Philippi and Kavala.
macedonia.credit: The Egnatian Way near Kavala. Photo: Philipp Pilhofer, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

miletus.text: Miletus is a ruin in western Turkey, now inland since its harbor silted up. Its large theatre still stands over the plain that was once the sea.
miletus.credit: The theatre at Miletus. Photo: Bernard Gagnon, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

ptolemais.text: Ptolemais is Acre, a walled port in northern Israel. Its Ottoman city on Crusader foundations is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

adria.text: The central Mediterranean between Crete, Greece and Sicily remains an open, storm-prone sea, crossed by modern shipping lanes.
adria.credit: A winter storm on the Ionian coast of Sicily. Photo: Jeanne Griffin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

antonia.text: The rock on which the Antonia stood is now the courtyard of the Umariyya school on the Via Dolorosa. Nearby, the Sisters of Sion show a Roman pavement once believed to be its courtyard.
antonia.credit: The Antonia in the model of 1st-century Jerusalem at the Israel Museum. Photo: Oren Rozen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

appiiforum.text: The Appian Way south of Rome still runs straight across the old Pontine Marshes, drained in the 1930s. Borgo Faiti stands near the ancient Forum of Appius.
appiiforum.credit: The Appian Way. Photo: Livioandronico2013, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

fairhavens.text: Kaloi Limenes is a quiet bay on the south coast of Crete, with a small chapel of St Paul on the shore and oil tanks on an islet.
fairhavens.credit: The bay of Kaloi Limenes, Crete. Photo: Olaf Tausch, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

malta.text: St Paul's Bay, in the north of Malta, is a resort town. St Paul's Islands, where the ship is thought to have struck, carry a statue of Paul set up in 1845.
malta.credit: St Paul's Islands, Malta. Photo: Berthold Werner, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

myra.text: Myra is near Demre in southern Turkey, with rock-cut Lycian tombs and a Roman theatre. The Church of St Nicholas, bishop of Myra, stands in the town.
myra.credit: Lycian rock tombs at Myra. Photo: Saffron Blaze, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

puteoli.text: Puteoli is Pozzuoli, near Naples. Its Roman market hall, long called the Temple of Serapis, shows the ground's rise and fall in the bands on its columns.
puteoli.credit: The Roman market hall at Pozzuoli. Photo: Norbert Nagel, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

rome.text: Rome is the capital of Italy and home of the Vatican. The ruins of the Forum and the Palatine lie in the heart of the city.
rome.credit: The Colosseum, Rome. Photo: Wilfredor, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

sidon.text: Sidon is Saida, a port city in southern Lebanon. Its Crusader Sea Castle stands on a small island joined to the shore by a stone causeway.
sidon.credit: The Sea Castle at Sidon. Photo: Vyacheslav Argenberg, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

syracuse.text: Syracuse is a city in south-east Sicily. Its old town on the island of Ortygia and its Greek theatre are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
syracuse.credit: Ortygia, the old town of Syracuse. Photo: Andrea Schaffer, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

zaragoza.text: Zaragoza is the capital of Aragón. The Basilica of Our Lady of the Pillar, built from 1681 with eleven domes and four towers, stands on the bank of the Ebro.
zaragoza.credit: The Basilica of Our Lady of the Pillar on the Ebro. Photo: Ymblanter, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

maryhouse.text: The House of the Virgin Mary is a small stone chapel among trees on the hill above Ephesus. Pilgrims tie prayer ribbons on a wall near the spring below it.
maryhouse.credit: The House of the Virgin Mary above Ephesus. Photo: Peter C in Toronto Canada, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

compostela.text: Santiago de Compostela's cathedral, finished in the 12th century and given its Baroque front in 1750, holds the apostle's tomb. More than 400,000 pilgrims a year now walk the Camino to it.
compostela.credit: A bell tower of the cathedral's Obradoiro front. Photo: Luis Miguel Bugallo Sánchez, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

dormition.text: The Dormition Abbey, a Benedictine church with a round tower, stands on Mount Zion just outside the Old City walls. Its crypt holds a stone figure of the Virgin asleep.
dormition.credit: The Dormition Abbey on Mount Zion. Photo: Godot13, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

marystomb.text: The Tomb of the Virgin is reached by a wide flight of steps down into the Kidron Valley, beneath a Crusader façade. Oil lamps hang in the dim church, which is shared by Greek Orthodox and Armenians.
marystomb.credit: The tomb chamber in the Church of the Tomb of the Virgin. Photo: WomEOS, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

muziris.text: Kodungallur is a town in Kerala. The Muziris Heritage Project has opened sites around Pattanam, and a church at Azhikode marks the traditional landing of St Thomas.

patras.text: Patras is Greece's third-largest city. The Basilica of St Andrew, finished in 1974, is the largest church in Greece and keeps relics of the apostle.
patras.credit: Inside the old church of St Andrew, Patras. Photo: Armineaghayan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

tarraco.text: Tarragona, on the coast of Catalonia, keeps its Roman amphitheatre by the sea, its circus and walls. They are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
tarraco.credit: The Roman amphitheatre at Tarragona. Photo: Bernard Gagnon, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

quovadis.text: The church of Domine Quo Vadis is a small chapel on the Appian Way in the Appia Antica park. Its present front dates from 1637.
quovadis.credit: The church of Domine Quo Vadis on the Appian Way. Photo: LPLT, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

vatican.text: St Peter's Basilica, built from 1506 to 1626, stands over the traditional tomb of Peter. Visitors can tour the excavations under the basilica in small groups.
vatican.credit: St Peter's Basilica. Photo: Alvesgaspar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

trefontane.text: The Abbey of Tre Fontane is a quiet Trappist monastery in the south of Rome. Its three churches include San Paolo alle Tre Fontane, with the three springs.
trefontane.credit: The Abbey of Tre Fontane. Photo: Fczarnowski, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

pella.text: Pella is a ruin at Tabaqat Fahl in northern Jordan, overlooking the Jordan Valley. Its Byzantine churches and Roman theatre lie below a hilltop rest house.
pella.credit: Ruins at Tabaqat Fahl, ancient Pella. Photo: Mohammad hajeer, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

mylapore.text: Mylapore is a busy old quarter of Chennai. The white San Thome Basilica, built in 1896, stands near the beach over the traditional tomb of St Thomas.
mylapore.credit: San Thome Basilica, Chennai. Photo: Pinakpani, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

hierapolis.text: Hierapolis sits above the white travertine terraces of Pamukkale, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The octagonal Martyrium of St Philip stands on the hillside above the ruins.
hierapolis.credit: The travertine terraces of Pamukkale below Hierapolis. Photo: Brocken Inaglory, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stjohn.text: The ruins of Justinian's Basilica of St John stand on Ayasuluk hill in Selçuk, below the citadel. Columns have been re-erected, and the tomb lies under a marble slab.
stjohn.credit: The ruins of the Basilica of St John, Selçuk. Photo: Dosseman, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

patmos.text: Patmos is a quiet island of about 3,000 people. The fortified Monastery of St John, founded in 1088, crowns Chora, and the Cave of the Apocalypse lies halfway down the hill.
